# Scope for growth of the sea urchin *Heliocidaris erythrogramma* under future warming and acidification

## Introduction

As maintaining energy surplus is the key for long-term survival, bioenergetics-based models can be used to examine how environmental stressors affect the fitness and survival of marine organisms by changing their energy budget.


## Methods 

### Collection
*Heliocidaris erythrogramma* (44.15 $\pm$ 3.25 *mm* test diameter) were collected by hand at the subtidal zone from Milk Beach ([-33.856478, 151.266958](https://www.google.com/maps/?q=-33.856478,151.266958)) and Bottle and Glass Point ([-33.847960, 151.270122](https://www.google.com/maps/?q=-33.847960,151.270122)) in June, 2014, when sea surface temperature (SST) was $15.3^{\circ}C$.
The urchins were transported to the Sydney Institute of Marine Science (SIMS) in Chowder Bay and held in aquaria ($80\ L$) supplied with ambient flow-through seawater (FSW, $70\ \mu m$, $1.5\ L\ min^{-1}$).
After 1 week, they were randomly allocated into treatment groups based on three temperature profiles (ambient: $+0^{\circ}C$, elevated: $+2^{\circ}C$ and $+3^{\circ}C$, adjusted weekly with regard to the mean SST profile as detailed below) and two constant total pH ($pH_T$, on the total hydrogen scale) levels (ambient $8.0$, acidic: $7.6$) in a fully orthogonal design (**Fig. 1**).

### Experimental setup

We performed all acclimation experiments in a constant-temperature room where the lighting was adjusted weekly to reflct the diurnal sunrise/sunset cycle.
Each header tank was supplied with FSW ($20\ \mu m$) using individual thermocouple-solenoid feedback systems that automatically mixed warm ($25^{\circ}C$) and cold ($14.5^{\circ}C$) filtered FSW ($20\ \mu m$) in a $2\ L$ mixing chamber to supply temperature-controlled water consistently.
Each header tank was also equipped with a heater (75 W, EHEIM GmbH & Co KG, Germany) attached to a temperature controller (model 7028/3, TUNZE Aqraientechnik GmbH, Germany) as a second level of temperature control.

Sea water pH was maintained using a mixed $CO_2$ system where a thermally-compensated, low-flow controller valve (Parker Hannifin, OH, USA) and a proportional–integral–derivative controller, updated every $10\ s$, were used to precisely inject food-grade $CO_2$ (BOC, Australia) into ambient air that had been scrubbed of $CO_2$.
The $CO_2$-mix was bubbled vigorously and continuously into header tanks via $20 cm$ ceramic diffusers.


#### Gradual adjustment to treatment conditions and acclimation

Each treatment consisted of three replicate tanks with 10 urchins per tank (total $n = 180$).
To minimise physiological shock to altered conditions, adjustments to the levels of warming and acidification of the tanks were performed gradually. 
Temperature was increased at a rate of $1^{\circ}C$ every 6 days until target elevated temperatures were achieved.
Sea water pH was decreased at a rate of $-0.1\ pH_T$ units every week.
Both temperature and pH manipulations were performed in a staggered schedule such that all treatments achieved target conditions in the same week (**Fig. \@ref(fig:acclim) A**).
We made all adjustments in header tanks such that treatments slowly stabilised to their new conditions within 1 to 2 days.
The adjustment process took 7 weeks, and no mortality was recorded during this period.
Once the treatment conditions were established, treatment temperatures were at $15.6 \pm 0.4^{\circ}C$, $17.6 \pm 0.4^{\circ}C$ and $18.6 \pm 0.3^{\circ}C$ (s.d.) for the ambient, $+2^{\circ}C$ and $+3^{\circ}C$ treatments respectively.

After the adjustment period, the urchins were subject to an acclimation protocol where temperature levels were regulated weekly based on an offset to previously-recorded mean weekly temperature from winter to summer temperatures in Sydney Harbour (**Fig. \@ref(fig:acclim) A \& B**). 
Thus treatment temperatures were adjusted weekly to mimic the seasonal change expected over winter to early summer. 
The temperatures were based on reference data collected from *in situ* loggers deployed in Chowder Bay from 2009–2014 (**Fig. \@ref(fig:harbour)**).
Because temperature has an effect on $CO_2$ solubility and temperatures were changing every week, the system maintained constant pH (not $CO_2$ ppm) within each treatment.
